newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's Werner sees no IMF deal for a while.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Werner sees no IMF deal for a while.

text.p: Mexico will wait until it has finished negotiations in Congress on its 1998 economic program before signing a new agreement with the International Monetary Fund, Deputy Finance Minister Martin Werner said on Tuesday.

"We're going to concentrate now on working on our 1998 economic program and working with the new Congress. After that we will see about putting the finishing touches on an extended fund facility with the IMF," he said in a Reuters interview.

Mexico's stand-by agreement with the IMF ended on schedule in February. Since then the Finance Ministry has insisted it is in no hurry to clinch a new deal because its has a moderate payments schedule until 1999, when $5.9 billion comes due.
Mexico still owes about the IMF about $10 billion, the remainder of a $17 billion rescue package issued to the country in 1995 when Mexico was on the verge of financial collapse.
The IMF wants eventually to complete a deal on an extended fund facility with Mexico, if only to maintain a formal relationship with one of its biggest debtors.
"It could happen in the next six to eight months," Werner said. "There's no sense of urgency."
He said Mexico's three-year economic program, known as Pronafide, had already received the IMF's blessing, and that fund officials were not pressing for a quick deal.
"They feel the program is going as they expected...and they are very relaxed about the way in which the economy is evolving. We don't feel from them a sense of urgency either," he said.

Mexico's economy grew 8.8 percent in the second quarter, much stronger than expected. Having restored a lustrous growth rate, the government's next challenge, economists say, is to negotiate a fiscally responsible 1998 budget in Congress.

For the first time in 68 years, opposition parties will dominate the lower house of Congress, beginning September 1. In the July 6 midterm elections, the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party suffered an unprecedented setback.
The opposition has called for tax cuts and an increase in social spending, but the Finance Ministry says it cannot afford to lower taxes.
